display_title: Perhaps they use Mixup instead of Gaussian?

content.title: Perhaps they use Mixup instead of Gaussian?
content.comment:
Thank you for your interest and feedback. In our paper, we mention that label smoothing and logit squeezing without Gaussian augmentation decrease robustness, as seen in our MNIST experiments (appendix) and as mentioned in Zantedeschi et al., 2017.  However, adding random gaussian noise augmentation during label smoothing (and logit squeezing) increases robustness. In fact, by using large smoothing and noise parameters, we are able to match or sometimes even beat adversarial training.  This motivated us to explore the effects of random gaussian augmentation (which we believe is a contributions of our paper)

While we were not able to find any random gaussian augmentations reported in the other paper you mention, we did notice that they use “mixup” when training a network using their method (LRM). From the accuracies they report on non-adversarial clean examples (Table1 in their paper), it seems likely that they use mixup when training with the other methods (including Label smoothing) as well. This would explain the accuracies they report;  the “Regular training” in Table1 of their paper achieves only 87.4% accuracy on “Natural” examples, while the Naturally trained model from Madry has 95.2% accuracy on clean test examples (Madry et al., 2018). Mixup may have the same “off-manifold” generalization property that gaussian augmentation has. But as it can be seen, it hurts the accuracy on clean examples. Our test accuracy is above 90% (using the same ResNet that Madry uses). While the test accuracy they report using LRM is 68.5%.

To be quantitative:  we just ran an experiment with label_smoothing=0.8 without any gaussian augmentation on CIFAR-10, and attacked it with a 20-step PGD attack on the CW loss.  The attack degrades the model accuracy to only  5%.

content.comment:
>> "The reason ALP seems to be doing better in Table 2 in the paper you posted is because you are comparing PGD training and ALP training for the same number of iterations."

Please note, that in Table 2 we already show the results for 10 and 400 iterations (n=10 and n=400 in our notation) of the PGD attack. This alone helped to reduce the adversarial accuracy quite significantly. Instead of increasing the number of iterations even further, we decided to rather go for multiple random restarts, which helped to reduce the adv. accuracy of the LSQ model from 7.0% to 1.7%. 
Note that at the same time the adv. accuracy of AT and ALP models essentially stayed the same. And since we observed the same effect on 3 datasets (MNIST, CIFAR-10, Tiny ImageNet), we think that this suggests that ALP may slightly increase actual robustness.
Also note, that Engstrom et al could completely break the open-sourced ImageNet model, because apparently, it was not a model trained with 50% AT + ALP, nor 100% AT + ALP.


>> "So run the ALP model for more number of steps and you should see it performing as good/bad as PGD."

Then there is a question about how many iterations are "many" :-) If a paper shows the results for X iterations of PGD attack, one can always ask about an attack with more iterations. This obviously reveals the problem with relying only on attacks to evaluate the robustness of classifiers. The evaluation of provable robustness seems like a good solution, although it has its own disadvantages.

content.title: As requested: more iterations
content.comment:
We chose a 20 iterations attack because this seems to be a common choice across many papers (including several submitted to ICLR 2019), and we wanted to replicate this standard experimental setting. 

That being said, it’s legitimate to wonder how this parameter effects results, and so we have run white-box experiments with increased numbers of PGD iterations.  We use the CW loss, which is the worst case for label smoothing and logit squeezing in our experiments.  Models were trained for 160K iterations (we see a trend of accuracy going up a bit with more iterations, but we cut off training here to keep things quick).  We used parameters logit_squeeze=10, and Gaussian noise with sigma=30.  These are the same parameters used in the paper for 20 steps; there may be something to be gained by optimizing these for 1000 step, but we have not had time to explore this.  
 
PGD Iterations		Accuracy
20			     	         49.73%
40				         45.33%
100				         42.36%
400				         41.58%
1000				 40.94%

It seems that running with more iterations does cause some loss in accuracy, although this effect seems to plateau.  We also ran some quick experiments with larger and smaller stepsizes, but found that this parameter had little effect on final performance.

Also, please note that white box performance isn’t everything.  Additional benefits of label smoothing and logit squeezing include:  
- Very high robustness in the black box setting and against non-iterative attacks
- High test accuracy on clean data
- Very fast training time compared to adversarial training

display_title: Will not stand up to scrutiny

content.title: Will not stand up to scrutiny
content.review:
This paper proposes using label smoothing and logit squeezing together with Gaussian noise injection at training time as a replacement for adversarial training. The paper builds on the flawed premise that label smoothing and logit squeezing can lead to more robustness - it simply masks the gradients so that the optimization landscape is harder. Also I am unconvinced that simply adding Gaussian noise together with these tricks can lead to any robustness against a worst case adversary - Gaussian noise augmentation is known to not lead to increased robustness (see e.g. [1]) while logit squeezing is also known to not lead to increased robustness (see e.g. [2]). So I cannot fathom why the two combined suddenly start working?

Also a glance at their experimental evaluation immediately uncovers the flaw that they only used 20 step PGD attack to evaluate the robustness of their model on CIFAR-10. Label smoothing and logit squeezing result in gradient masking and a more difficult terrain to optimize over, so increasing the number of attack steps and doing many random restarts will reveal that their claimed model is not as robust as the authors think.

[1] https://arxiv.org/pdf/1711.08478.pdf
[2] https://arxiv.org/pdf/1807.10272.pdf

content.title: Added experiments with stronger attacks, many restarts and pgd steps, and 100 classes.  Also added plots of the loss landscape
content.comment:
In citing reference [2], the reviewer has mistaken logit PAIRING (the topic of [2]) with logit SQUEEZING (our topic).  This is perhaps an easy mistake to make - several other commenters on this paper seem to have conflated the two.

We respectfully disagree with some of the comments from the reviewer, and feel that this review contains a number of overly strong and unjustified claims.  We are not aware of any analysis on the loss landscape of models that use label smoothing, and our (many) experiments are not compatible with the hypothesis that all logit-squeezed models are just masking gradients. In fact, at the request of one of the commenters, we have performed experiments with 1000-step PGD attacks and “infinite” epsilons, which are a common test for gradient masking (which our methods passed).

While gaussian data augmentation by itself is claimed not to boost robustness [1], it was recently claimed by Kannan, Kurakin, and Goodfellow (NIPS 2018 - https://arxiv.org/pdf/1803.06373.pdf ) that it does increase robustness. That being said, we agree with the reviewer insofar that Gaussian augmentation, by itself, is not a very effective way to harden classifiers to attacks.  We even show this in our experiments.  We leverage gaussian augmentation because of its synergistic interaction with other adversarial training methods, and we think the synergistic relationship is now widely accepted by the community.   In section 4, we state that the addition of gaussian augmentation to logit squeezing and label smoothing helps in two ways: it helps enforce regularization off the manifold, which is important for PGD multi-iterative attacks that move off the manifold after one-step (or even before the first step when they add the random initialization); Also, Gaussian augmentation synegerallistically interacts with the regularizers. For example, in figures 3 and 8, we show that gaussian noise + the regularizers squash the gradients even further (decrease the denominator of the analytical epsilon from equation 4).

We have added cross-entropy loss plots for the model that we consistently use to answer all questions.  We should note that the plots are for OUR logit-squeezed model. We believe that following the recommendations in our paper (please see reviewer 2's response for the recommendations for hyper-parameter selection)  yields such results -- applying logit squeezing with gaussian augmentation incorrectly without following our suggestions may not result in such loss landscapes.  In the revision, we have provided plots for the first 8 images of the validation set. The image pixels are modified along either two randomly (Rademacher(0.5)) chosen directions or along one random direction and one adversarial direction. From these plots, it seems that the loss landscape has not become convoluted. This observation is backed up by the fact that increasing the number of PGD attack steps beyond 400 does not substantially affect accuracy.
Plots for one random and one adversarial direction are presented in Fig. 9 in the appendix of the revised manuscript. 
Plots for both random directions can also be found in the revised manuscript (Fig. 5).

Our original submission reported results using a standard setup used in most studies (including many submitted to ICLR 2019). For MNIST the most common setup is 40-steps PGD and for CIFAR-10 this seems to be 20-steps. This being said, we agree that it is worth looking at how stronger attacks (more PGD steps and various random restarts) affect the performance.
In the revision, we have provided additional experiments on the logit squeezing=10, Gaussian augmentation std=30 model, which is trained for 160k iterations. It should be noted that attacking with more iterations and more random restarts hurts the adversarially trained models as well (see the leaderboard in https://github.com/MadryLab/cifar10_challenge ). The results for many PGD steps (up to 1000 steps) are found in our response to question 1 of reviewer 2. Our results using multiple random restarts are:

No. of random restarts       accuracy
-------------------------------------------------
               1                    |        52.30%
               2                    |        50.84%
               3                    |        50.43%
               4                    |        50.24%
               5                    |        50.21%
               6                    |        50.13%
               7                    |        50.04%
               8                    |        49.86%
               9                    |        49.86%

Similar to the Madry adversarially trained model, with more random restarts, there is a small drop in accuracy with more restarts. 

[1] https://arxiv.org/pdf/1711.08478.pdf
[2] https://arxiv.org/pdf/1807.10272.pdf

replying_to: Replying to Label Smoothing and Logit Squeezing: A Replacement for Adversarial Training?
display_title: Interesting results on CIFAR-10, but how conclusive are they?

content.title: Interesting results on CIFAR-10, but how conclusive are they?
content.review:
The paper addresses a highly relevant problem in Adversarial Machine Learning: devising alternatives to adversarial training that scale to high-dimensional datasets.

The proposed approach is a combination of known techniques: label smoothing, logit squeezing and Gaussian data augmentation. While those techniques had previously been studied in isolation, the authors argue that the combination thereof "saves the day", i.e. yielding high accuracy on clean data samples while exhibiting robustness against adversarial inputs.

The authors evaluate their approach on the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets. They compare against the adversarially trained and publicly available models by Madry et al (ICLR 2018). The results are mixed: on MNIST, Madry's model clearly outperforms the proposed approach in terms of adversarial robustness. On CIFAR-10, for a certain combination of logit squeezing and Gaussian data augmentation, the authors report results suggesting that their approach outperforms Madry's model both in terms of accuracy on clean samples and robustness against adversarial samples (white- and black-box). Specifically, the (alpha=0, beta=0, sigma=30, k=160k)-model in Table 3 achieves 90.5% accuracy on clean test samples (compared to Madry's 87.3%), 49.7% under white-box attacks (compared to 45.8%), and 67.0% under black-box attacks (compared to 64.2%).

Overall, a lot of the material in this manuscript didn't strike me as particularly deep or original. For instance, I am not convinced by the analysis "What does adversarial training do?" (Section 1) which is based on a linearity assumption, 
the importance of which isn't properly discussed.

The proposed alternative to adversarial training seems a bit unprincipled: the building blocks had been there before, but it appears the combination with specific parameter choices does the trick. It is a bit disconcerting that the approach doesn't perform that well for MNIST. A key selling point of the proposed approach is its computational efficiency; from that regard it would have been nice to see results on large-scale datasets like ImageNet. 

Having said all this, if the findings on CIFAR-10 indeed hold true, then I think this is an important result that is worth publishing at ICLR. It would indicate important directions for future research besides the mainstream work on adversarial training.

One concern that I have though is whether the CIFAR-10 models trained by the authors can withstand a wider range of attacks. To put it into perspective: Madry et al - in their CIFAR-10 challenge (https://github.com/MadryLab/cifar10_challenge) - report 44.71% accuracy under white-box attacks as the worst-case result *under any epsilon-bounded attack* that researchers have tried since this model was published about a year ago. The 49.7% accuracy for the (alpha=0, beta=0, sigma=30, k=160k)-model in Table 3 is the worst-case result under only 4 different attacks. One has to question: what would the worst-case result for this model be in one year from now if the community had white-box access to it?

Is there any way the authors could make their models publicly available during the review period?

One specific question: Madry's 46.8% accuracy under the CW attack was obtained for 30-step PGD. Table 3 states that only 20-step PGD was performed. Can the authors shed more light on what exact setup they used for the CW attack and what - if not reported in Table 3 - was the result under a 30-step attack?

A minor comment:
- Figure 2 (a) vs Footnote 1: was 20- or 40-step PGD being used?
content.rating: 4: Ok but not good enough - rejection
content.confidence: 3: The reviewer is fairly confident that the evaluation is correct

content.title: Thank you. We have performed extra experiments and stronger attacks against our models.
content.comment:
Thank you for your valuable feedback. Below please find our detailed response to your comments and concerns:

Reviewer: Overall, a lot of the material in this manuscript didn't strike me as particularly deep or original. For instance, I am not convinced by the analysis "What does adversarial training do?" (Section 1) which is based on a linearity assumption, the importance of which isn't properly discussed.

The meat of this paper is really our experimental results, and the observation that regularization methods can be competitive with adversarial training for hardening networks.  However, we don’t like our papers to be totally empirical; we think it’s important to try to understand why we get the results we do.  Unfortunately, the theory of adversarial training is highly under-developed, and so we investigate these issues through the lense of the linearized model, which is the sharpest tool we have.  Using this linearity assumption and the resulting analytical epsilon, we try to analyze how one can achieve robustness by manipulating the numerator or denominator of equation 4. We have used this metric to show how each of the ingredients work independently and together in order to achieve robustness. For each of the methods described and analyzed in the paper, we have provided an “epsilon plot” which includes the numerator, denominator, and our analytical epsilon.  Once again, the purpose of these plots is not to advance the state of the art in adversarial training, but rather to give the reader some insight into what’s going on.

-------------------------------------------------
Reviewer: A key selling point of the proposed approach is its computational efficiency; from that regard it would have been nice to see results on large-scale datasets like ImageNet. 

We agree that it is promising to use these regularizers on larger data-sets. However, achieving good white-box robustness plus higher clean accuracy on the well-studied models by itself are promising. At the reviewers request (above), we have provided new results on CIFAR-100 which are very promising. For a complete analysis, please see our response to reviewer 2.  Unfortunately, we do not at this time have the computational resources for training hardened models on ImageNet, and so we hope results on this more complex 100-class problem will suffice.

-------------------------------------------------
Reviewer: If the findings on CIFAR-10 indeed hold true, then I think this is an important result that is worth publishing at ICLR. It would indicate important directions for future research besides the mainstream work on adversarial training.

Please note that we have further reinforced the results in paper with results after attacking the models with multiple PGD steps (up to 1000 steps -- provided in response to reviewer 2) and multiple restarts on CIFAR-10 (see response to reviewer 1), in addition to the analysis of why these methods work. To top that off, our new results on CIFAR-100 (see reviewer 2’s response) are very promising which show that this method can be extended to cases where we have many classes.

-------------------------------------------------
Reviewer: Is there any way the authors could make their models publicly available during the review period?

We have been instructed not to provide links to github or google drive accounts to preserve anonymity.  Although since the reviewer has explicitly asked for sharing the saved models, out of respect, we have published our checkpoint file for the saved hardened wide Resnet-28 model using an anonymous link: https://drive.google.com/file/d/197Y21S19Hep5o5ON8zew6VRf86oR_IUj/view . The model is similar to that of Madry’s and can be loaded in the same fashion instructed in their CIFAR-10 challenge repo. 
It should be noted we are planning a full code release when the review process is complete.

-------------------------------------------------
Reviewer: One specific question: Madry's 46.8% accuracy under the CW attack was obtained for 30-step PGD. Table 3 states that only 20-step PGD was performed. Can the authors shed more light on what exact setup they used for the CW attack and what - if not reported in Table 3 - was the result under a 30-step attack? 

We originally chose 20-step PGD attacks on both the cross-entropy loss and the CW loss since it seems that this is the most common standard. However, at the request of reviewer, we have repeated our experiment with 30 step of PGD. The accuracy we get on a 30-step PGD attack on the CW loss for the model trained for 160k iterations with logit-squeezing=10, Gaussian augmentation std=30, is 47.13%.

-------------------------------------------------
Reviewer: A minor comment:- Figure 2 (a) vs Footnote 1: was 20- or 40-step PGD being used?

We used the 40-step PGD trained. Thanks for pointing  this out. We have fixed it in the revised document.

replying_to: Replying to Label Smoothing and Logit Squeezing: A Replacement for Adversarial Training?
display_title: Nice motivation and impressive empirical result. More experiments needed.

content.title: Nice motivation and impressive empirical result. More experiments needed.
content.review:
This paper studies training adversarially robust models without generating adversarial examples online during training. This way, the training time can be significantly reduced. Firstly, the authors draw inspiration from linear (approximation of) classifier and work out the epsilon_L formula. Based on this, the authors proposes three ways of making the model more robust. And specifically, the authors focus on label smoothing and logit squeezing, because both of them have an effect of reducing the logit gap and shrinking the logit. Coupled with Gaussian Noise trick, both methods work pretty well. On MNIST, it come, to some extent, close to PGD7 trained models. On CIAFR10, using aggressive smoothing or squeezing hyper-parameters, it surpasses PGD7 trained models.

1. On Table 3, I would like to see PGD-100 steps and PGD-200 steps for xent loss and CW loss.

2. From Table 2,3,4, it seems like the accuracy varies a lot when the hyper-parameter changes. Is there a good rule of thumb on how to set up a good hyper-parameters in case of a new dataset? 

3. Have you checked if the accuracy goes down as the perturbation budget epsilon goes up, say 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, using PGD20 or stronger attacks?

4. I would like to see results on CIFAR100, which is a harder dataset, containing 100 classes and 500 images per class. I think CIFAR10 alone is not sufficient for empirical justification nowadays (maybe it is enough one year ago). I don't know how the accuracy becomes under aggressive \alpha and \beta settings for 100-way classification. Also, evaluate them using PGD20, PGD100, PGD200 in order to make rigorous claims.

5. It seems that Gaussian trick is the key to good performance. Have you tried other form of random noise? Uniform or Laplace?

####### post-rebuttal

I have read the authors' reply, and other relevant comments in this page.  I am satisfied with the rebuttal. The weak point of this paper is 1) building blocks are all existing techniques so the overall method looks like tricks; 2) lack of explanation and understanding of why it works.  But I think this is a good empirical paper. It is true that nowadays there are many papers on this topic coming up, sometimes making contradictory claims (by using different experiment setup), but I am convinced by the results in the paper and in the rebuttal. Examining and running the released code would be better but that would take me too much time and effort.  I think the results are interesting and impressive. It tells the community something new. An important future study would be understanding why it works, and if (or how) it may implicitly inherently relate to adversarial training or regularization or other training methods for defense. Also, extending to ImageNet1000 would be very important. Given the CIFAR100 results, I am worried that smoothing or squeezing alone may not be readily working.

Thank you for your helpful comments. We believe that your comments have helped us in proving the robustness of our models even further. Below is our detailed response to some of your questions.
1. "On Table 3, I would like to see PGD-100 steps and PGD-200 steps for xent loss and CW loss."

We were not able to fit the results for PGD-100 and PGD-200 in Table 3. However, per your request, we have ran PGD with many more steps. To accompany your concern and those from the community, we have ran PGD with up to 1000 steps. Here are the results of white-box attacking the robust CIFAR-10 model with parameters logit_squeeze=10, and Gaussian noise with sigma=30 which was trained for 160K iterations (One of the models reported in the paper).

PGD Iterations		Accuracy
20                                       49.73%
40                                       45.33%
100                                     42.36%
400                                     41.58%
1000                                   40.94%

While there can be seen a drop in accuracy as we increase the number of PGD steps (i.e., make the attack stronger), the accuracy has plateaued and therefore we do not expect it to decrease significantly by increasing the number of iterations. 
We would like to reiterate that we believe white box performance isn’t everything. We have tried to revise the document to emphasize this. Additional benefits of label smoothing and logit squeezing include:  
- Very high robustness in the black box setting (roughly 3% higher than that for adversarial training per Table 4 ) and against white-box non-iterative (or less iterative) attacks (roughly 15% Per Table 3)
- High test accuracy on clean data (roughly 3% per Table 3)
- Very fast training time compared to adversarial training (roughly 4 times faster even for the models trained for 160k iterations)

2. "From Table 2,3,4, it seems like the accuracy varies a lot when the hyper-parameter changes. Is there a good rule of thumb on how to set up a good hyper-parameters in case of a new dataset?"

Based on our (large) number of experiments we notice that as we increase the number of training iterations, we get more robust models for both logit squeezing and label smoothing. Generally, we get more robust models when we use larger smoothing ($\alpha$) and squeezing ($\beta$) parameters, and when Gaussian augmentation is used with standard deviation $\sigma$ that is greater than the desired $\epsilon$ (the maximum perturbation size).
Based on our experiments, increasing $\beta$ and $\alpha$ increases robustness (provided that we do enough training) until some point where the classification loss becomes irrelevant. 
Based on these observations, our general framework for choosing hyper-parameters is this:  we select the largest regularization values we can while maintaining 100% train accuracy and cross-entropy loss should be less than 2. Note that it is possible to have large cross-entropy loss values and still maintain about 100% accuracy. In this case, the adversary has an easy task and only needs to change the cross entropy by a tiny amount (pass it over the threshold) to cause misclassification. For example one of our newly trained models for CIFAR-100 (logit_squeeze=10, Gauss_std=20, k=160 ) has 100% training accuracy and about 70% validation accuracy but we can make adversarial examples for it even with small epsilon budgets (epsilon=4) because the cross-entropy loss for training and validation on the clean examples are about 2.3, and 3.3, respectively . Generally, it is possible to satisfy the confidence part at the expense of computation time by increasing the number of iterations and decreasing the step-size.

3. "Have you checked if the accuracy goes down as the perturbation budget epsilon goes up, say 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, using PGD20 or stronger attacks?"

Yes, we have verified that increasing the attack budget causes the accuracy to drop. This sanity check verifies that our attack is not benefiting from obfuscating the gradients. Here are the results for attacking the model used as reference in our response to question 1:
Iterations	step-size	epsilon		accuracy
     30                           2		    50		  14.48%
     40                           2		    60		  9.02%
     50                           3		   100		  2.07%
     50                           4		   150		  0.22%
     100                         4		   150		  0.13%
     200                         2		   255		  0.00%

4. "I would like to see results on CIFAR100, which is a harder dataset, containing 100 classes and 500 images per class. I think CIFAR10 alone is not sufficient for empirical justification nowadays (maybe it is enough one year ago). I don't know how the accuracy becomes under aggressive \alpha and \beta settings for 100-way classification. Also, evaluate them using PGD20, PGD100, PGD200 in order to make rigorous claims."

Per your suggestion, we have trained models using aggressive label-smoothing and logit squeezing on CIFAR-100. We have used the same Wide resnet with depth 28 and k=10 that was used for CIFAR-10 and have used the common data-augmentation schemes with weight-decay similar to that for CIFAR-10. Here are some preliminary results on CIFAR-100:

logit-squeeze-coef     rand-std    iters    PGD-7     PGD-20    PGD-100     PGD-200
              0                            0            80k      0.02%       0.00%         -                      -
              1                           20           80k     16.37%      8.19%         -                      -
              1                           20          160k    30.72%    23.89%         -                      - 
              5                           20           80k     30.68%    22.91%      18.69%         18.09%
              5                           20          160k    37.08%    30.91%      26.47%         26.00%

2-step PGD adv trained                            20.08%    17.08%      16.50%         16.49%

Against 7-step attacks, our logit squeezed model achieves 37.08% accuracy when the best parameters are used (which, btw, are in line with the hyper-parameter rule of thumb stated above).  Benchmarks on adversarial training for CIFAR-100 do not seem to be common in the published literature.  The one published benchmark we found to compare against was Buckman et al. (https://openreview.net/pdf?id=S18Su--CW), who achieve 6.02% robustness against PGD-7 attacks using a wide resnet model. Using our setup,  we were able to improve over this adversarial training benchmark using a 2-step PGD adversary (similar to Madry) on the wide-resnet 28 k=10 network, which achieves 20.08% accuracy against a 7-step attack.  Due to time constraints and a lack of GPUs in our academic lab, we do not yet have results with 7-step adversarial training.  We would point out, though, that creating this model with 2-step PGD adversarial training already took considerably long (34.3 hours). Training our logit squeezed model (160k iterations) takes 28.8 hours.

We have reported the results for PGD-100 and PGD-200 attacks on the best model per your request. As it can be seen, the accuracy seems to have plateaued and is not decreasing much as we increase the number of iterations beyond 100 steps.

5. "It seems that Gaussian trick is the key to good performance. Have you tried other form of random noise? Uniform or Laplace?"
We have done limited experiments with uniform noise, but initial results were not promising and we chose not to pursue this direction further.  We have not yet tried Laplace noise - this is an interesting direction and will be investigated for future work!

display_title: Logit squeezing is (indeed) not robust

content.comment:
I would like to point you to our paper https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.12042 where we show that logit squeezing (combined with gaussian noise), as proposed by Harini et al., does not provide actual robustness. We could successfully break it on MNIST, CIFAR10 and Tiny ImageNet. Further, we find that the robustness of logit squeezing mainly comes from the fact that it makes gradient based optimization in the input space significantly more difficult by introducing many local maxima near the clean inputs. This can be seen as gradient masking. Crucial for our evaluation was the fact that we performed many random restarts when performing PGD (up to 10000) and additionally performed a proper grid search over the step size used during optimization. So just increasing the number of iterations (as mentioned in the comments below) might not be sufficient to break a defense that significantly alters the input space loss surface. 

Therefore, it would be interesting to see the robustness of your models against a PGD attack with large number of iterations, large step size, and many random restarts. Based on our experiments, this should reduce the adversarial accuracy of these models down to (almost) 0%.

content.comment:
Hi Marius,
Apart from using a different choice of architectures than ours (we use the wide resnet from Madry et al., 2018 for comparison purposes), your experiments use very different parameter settings than our setup.   One of our goals is to reveal how changes in these parameters affect robustness and performance, and we show that fairly unusual parameter choices are needed to achieve good robustness.   For consistency, we ultimately use one parameter setting to respond to all queries about our work so as to avoid cherry picking results. Below are some of the differences we noted between the parameters used in your paper and the one setting we are using:

Paper			|  Mosbach et al.		|      	Us
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Epsilon                   |        16 (0.062)	        |         8 (0.031)
Stdev noise           |              0.06	                |     0.1176 (i.e. 30/255) 
Logit_squeeze      |              0.25		        |              10
Trainingsteps       |    100*50k/128=39k	|             160k
 
Several of the differences in our setups are discussed below...
-  In your experiments, the std_noise/epsilon ratio is about 1 while our’s is 3.75. As seen in our Table 6 (appendix), we do not get much robustness when this ratio is small. For good results, you need stdev of the noise to be larger than epsilon.
- Your regularization parameter is 40X smaller than ours.  Our paper states that “aggressive logit squeezing” yields better robustness, and we show that robustness generally increases as we increase this coefficient. When the coefficient gets large enough, we start to sacrifice accuracy and training time, which is why we stop at 10.
- We use an adversary with epsilon=8. This has become standard, and enables broad comparisons against other defenses in the literature.  While defending against larger perturbations is an interesting direction of active research, we do not try this in our paper.
- Your training methods only uses 100 epochs (approx 39K iters), which is small.  For example Madry’s adversarial training uses 200 epochs (much more than for natural training). Intuitively, it seems that training against a larger epsilon (16) as you did, would require more training iterations.

There are also a few irregularities we noticed in your results.  On resnet-20 v2 you report 83% accuracy on natural training while v1 of this network gets 91% (He et al., 2015).  We are using standard data augmentation and weight decay (similar to Madry et al.) but perhaps you are not using these methods when training? 

Finally, we ran additional experiments with random restarts to see if it degrades accuracy as you claim.  We get the following accuracies against a 20-step PGD attack on the cross entropy loss.

Random restarts      |      accuracy
-------------------------------------------------
               1                   |        52.30%
               2                   |        50.84%
               3                   |        50.43%
               4                   |        50.24%
               5                   |        50.21%
               6                   |        50.13%
               7                   |        50.04%
               8                   |        49.86%
               9                   |        49.86%

It seems that, at least for modest numbers of restarts, robustness is not significantly impacted by restarts.
